tool_args.old_string: This pattern supports the implicit regularization hypothesis: evidence generation forces smaller models to attend to supporting context, reducing degenerate repetition. tool_args.new_string: Two mechanisms may explain this pattern. The parsimonious account is a structural output constraint: evidence formatting occupies token budget, leaving fewer tokens for triples, which reduces false positives and duplicates---a purely output-level effect. However, under matched@2048 evaluation where truncation is controlled, the 1.7B evidence benefit persists ($-$5.63pp), partially challenging a pure output-constraint explanation and suggesting a possible representation-level effect where evidence generation encourages the model to attend to supporting context. Our data cannot distinguish the relative contributions of these two mechanisms; controlled experiments with fixed output length but varied evidence requirements would be needed. At 4B, duplication is already moderate (31.1\% with evidence), so either mechanism's benefit diminishes; under matched@2048 evaluation, the 4B training-time tax is approximately neutral (+0.25$\pm$0.47pp, three-seed mean). The truncation asymmetry reverses across scales: at 1.7B the no-evidence model truncates 19pp more often; at 8B the evidence model truncates 9pp more often due to the longer output format.

tool_args.command: echo "Large Language Model (LLM)-based Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) now matches or exceeds encoder baselines in extraction accuracy, yet these methods output bare relation triplets without identifying supporting sentences. Encoder-based evidence methods (SAIS, DREEAM) provide supporting sentences but trail LLM approaches in accuracy, creating a gap between extraction performance and output verifiability. We formalize evidence-grounded DocRE as structured generation and compare Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), and Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning (RSFT) across three fully evaluated scales (1.7B, 4B, 8B) with 14B validation, two model families, and two datasets. The evidence tax extraction cost of generating evidence is scale-dependent beneficial at 1.7B but approximately neutral at 4B positive cost. Gradient-based optimization amplifies evidence-extraction competition GRPO catastrophic DPO gradual while RSFT with Natural Language Inference NLI based scoring avoids decoupling entirely through output filtering rather than gradient pressure. We introduce the Evidence-Decoupling Ratio EDCR to quantify extraction-evidence misalignment validated at per-relation level. Our 1.7B RSFT model 51.19 Ign-F1 approaches 8B Supervised Fine-Tuning SFT performance 50.19 at 4.7 fewer parameters. Test-set evaluation preserves model ranking across all evaluated scales Spearman rho 1.0." | wc -w

37	\paragraph{RSFT.}
38	Rejection Sampling Fine-Tuning is a single-round variant of iterative self-improvement methods such as STaR~\citep{zelikman2022star}. The procedure is straightforward: the SFT model generates $N{=}8$ candidate outputs per training document, each candidate is scored by CED, and only the top-$k{=}1$ response is retained as training data. We use $k{=}1$ (best-of-$N$) selection throughout all experiments, selecting the single highest-scoring candidate per document for RSFT training data construction. This yields approximately 3,000 training examples per model (one per document; exact counts vary slightly by model due to generation failures). Unlike GRPO and DPO, RSFT does not apply gradient-based optimization pressure toward a reward signal. Instead, it improves training data quality through filtering: the model trains on its own best outputs rather than all outputs. This distinction is critical because discrete selection over complete outputs cannot exploit the extraction-evidence trade-off that gradient methods find. The contribution of RSFT in our setting is not the framework itself, which is well-established, but its application to evidence-grounded DocRE with CED as a domain-specific quality filter.

153	The 1.7B evidence tax comparison (\S\ref{sec:scaling}) is confounded by differential truncation rates. At \texttt{max\_new\_tokens}$=$1024, the no-evidence model truncates 50.9\% of outputs (501/985 documents) versus 31.9\% (314/985) for the evidence model. To address this, we adopt a matched@2048 fair evaluation: both configurations are evaluated at \texttt{max\_new\_tokens}$=$2048, and the tax is computed on the intersection of documents where both produce format-compliant output. This yields 971/985 fair-subset documents, with a tax of $-$5.63pp (s42), confirming a genuine 1.7B evidence benefit.
